items.question:
An insurance compliance analyst uses Claude each week to review newly published regulatory circulars. Each session she pastes the same context: which jurisdiction she covers, that outputs must cite specific regulatory sections, and that language must be suitable for a board-level summary. The setup takes 5 minutes every time. A colleague suggests creating a Claude Project.

What is the PRIMARY justification for creating a Project here?

options.A: The recurring per-session setup cost — re-entering the same context each week — justifies encoding that context once in project instructions.
options.B: A Project is required whenever Claude must cite specific regulatory sections, because citations cannot be activated without project-level configuration.
options.C: A Project is only justified if the analyst shares the work with at least two other team members.
options.D: The analyst should create a Project only when a single session exceeds 30 minutes of work.

items.question:
A bid manager at an engineering consultancy created a Claude Project for proposal writing with the instruction: 'Write high-quality, persuasive proposals that win business.' After two months, the team finds that some proposals are too short, some use the wrong section structure, and some adopt an academic tone unsuitable for commercial clients.

What is the ROOT CAUSE of these inconsistencies?

options.A: The project instruction is too long and Claude is selectively applying parts of it each session.
options.B: The instruction is aspirational rather than operational — it describes a desired outcome without specifying length, structure, or tone, leaving Claude to interpret each dimension independently.
options.C: The instruction conflicts with Claude's default behaviour for commercial writing, which prioritises academic register.
options.D: Proposal format instructions must be placed in the knowledge base rather than the custom instructions for consistent application.

items.question:
A grant writer at a non-profit has a Claude Project with the instruction: 'All funding summaries should use headers, bullet points, and a maximum of 400 words.' For a specific funder that requires narrative prose with no bullet points and no word limit, she writes in her chat: 'The funder requires narrative prose — no bullet points, no word limit. Please write accordingly.'

How will Claude MOST likely respond?

options.A: Claude will use headers and bullet points as specified in the project instruction, since format specifications take precedence over per-chat requests.
options.B: Claude will ask the grant writer to update the project instruction before adopting narrative prose.
options.C: Claude will write in narrative prose without bullet points and without applying the 400-word limit, following the explicit per-chat format instruction for this session.
options.D: Claude will produce two versions — one in the project format and one in narrative prose — so the grant writer can choose.

items.question:
A RevOps analyst at a SaaS startup has created four Claude Projects over three months: one for CRM data analysis, one for sales email templates, one for pipeline forecasting, and one for customer health scoring. She named them: 'Claude Project,' 'New Project,' 'Project – Sales,' and 'Test Project.'

Which naming principle would MOST improve her ability to use these Projects effectively?

options.A: Rename Projects with sequential numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) so they sort predictably in the interface.
options.B: Rename all Projects to match the department they support (e.g., 'Revenue Operations').
options.C: Rename Projects to be as short as possible to reduce visual clutter in the Project list.
options.D: Rename each Project to reflect its specific function (e.g., 'CRM Analysis,' 'Sales Email Templates') so the correct Project is identifiable at a glance.

items.question:
A procurement manager at a professional services firm is setting up a Claude Project for a team of six junior analysts writing supplier assessment reports. She has 15 years of procurement experience and knows exactly what a rigorous supplier assessment should contain: specific risk categories, evidence standards, and recommendation language. She asks whether to put this knowledge in the project instructions.

What is the BEST rationale for encoding her expertise in the project instructions?

options.A: Once encoded in project instructions, her expert standards automatically apply to every analyst's session — making senior expertise available consistently at scale without requiring her to review each report.
options.B: Project instructions are the only way to prevent junior analysts from accessing Claude without proper guidance.
options.C: Claude cannot produce specialist procurement output without first receiving instructions from a domain expert in the project setup.
options.D: Project instructions prevent analysts from overriding her standards via per-chat prompts, ensuring rigid compliance.

items.question:
A clinical coordinator at a pharma company uses a Claude Project for investigator site queries. The Project has a custom instruction specifying the required response format and regulatory citation style. She uploads a site-specific protocol deviation summary in Monday's chat and references it throughout that conversation. On Wednesday she starts a new chat in the same Project.

What will be available in Wednesday's chat?

options.A: Both the custom instructions and the site-specific protocol deviation summary she uploaded on Monday.
options.B: Only the custom instructions; the uploaded protocol deviation summary was part of Monday's chat and is not available in a new session unless she uploads it again.
options.C: Only the protocol deviation summary; custom instructions must be re-entered in each new conversation.
options.D: Neither — Projects reset completely between sessions to protect confidential clinical data.

items.question:
An internal communications manager at a financial services firm is setting up a Claude Project for producing all-staff announcements. The company brand voice guidelines specify: warm but professional, avoid corporate jargon, use active voice, and always close with a forward-looking statement connecting to the company's mission. She writes the instruction: 'Write in our company's brand voice.'

Why is this instruction likely to produce inconsistent results?

options.A: Brand voice instructions must be uploaded to the knowledge base, not entered as custom instructions.
options.B: Claude cannot access company brand guidelines unless they are stored in its training data.
options.C: The instruction does not specify the actual brand voice attributes — warmth, jargon prohibition, active voice, required closing — so Claude cannot reliably apply them without knowing what the brand voice is.
options.D: Tone instructions require at least three example outputs for Claude to calibrate correctly; without examples, the instruction will be ignored.

items.question:
A legal operations analyst at a law firm has a Claude Project with instructions specifying: formal legal register, three-section memo structure (issue, analysis, recommendation), and a required citation of the governing jurisdiction at the start of each memo. A partner asks for a quick informal summary for an internal Slack message and adds in the chat: 'Keep this conversational — it's just for Slack, not a formal memo.'

Which TWO statements accurately describe what will happen? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude will adopt a conversational register for this response, since the per-chat instruction explicitly addresses the tone dimension.
options.B: The three-section memo structure (issue, analysis, recommendation) may be relaxed or collapsed in a conversational Slack response, since a Slack format implicitly overrides document structure requirements.
options.C: The formal register will be retained regardless, since legal register is a protected category that per-chat instructions cannot override.
options.D: The per-chat instruction addresses tone ('conversational') but does not explicitly address the three-section structure or jurisdiction citation, so those elements may still appear unless further per-chat guidance excludes them.
options.E: Claude will refuse to write the Slack message because the project instruction requires formal memos and a Slack format conflicts with that requirement.

items.question:
A customer success VP at a SaaS company shares a Claude Project with eight customer success managers. The Project has detailed instructions for writing executive business reviews (EBRs): required sections, data interpretation standards, recommended action frameworks, and tone guidelines for executive stakeholders. Before the Project, EBR quality varied significantly across the team. Six months after rollout, the VP reviews EBR outputs and finds they are now highly consistent in structure and tone. She wants to measure the business impact.

Which outcome MOST directly demonstrates the business value of the shared Project's standardisation?

options.A: The VP now spends less time editing individual EBRs, freeing capacity for strategic work.
options.B: The CSMs report higher satisfaction with their work because they no longer spend time deciding on format.
options.C: Customer renewal rates have increased since EBRs became more consistent, suggesting that clearer executive communication improved perceived value.
options.D: The team requires less onboarding time for new CSMs because the Project encodes the standard previously held in the VP's head, reducing reliance on her direct training.

items.question:
A financial analyst at a hedge fund has built a Claude Project for investment research summaries. After nine months of adding instructions, the set now has 52 individual rules covering formatting, citation style, disclaimer language, risk categorisation, investment thesis framing, and 23 edge cases for unusual securities. She notices outputs are increasingly inconsistent, with some rules appearing to be ignored.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the increased inconsistency?

options.A: A 52-rule instruction set exceeds the practical density at which all rules are applied consistently — rules begin to conflict, create ambiguity, or compete for priority, causing inconsistent application across sessions.
options.B: After nine months of continuous use, the Project's instruction cache degrades and must be cleared and the instructions re-entered to restore consistent behaviour.
options.C: The 52 rules are processed sequentially and Claude applies only the most recently added rules, ignoring earlier ones as new rules are added.
options.D: The inconsistency is caused by the 23 edge case instructions, which should have been placed in the knowledge base rather than the custom instructions.

items.question:
An inventory analyst at a retail chain needs Claude to help her write a one-time data quality audit report for a board presentation next week. She has never used Claude for this type of task before, has no plans to repeat it, and will provide all the specific data and context in her prompt. A colleague suggests she create a Claude Project for it.

Is the colleague's suggestion appropriate?

options.A: Yes — any Claude task should be managed through a Project to ensure quality and accountability.
options.B: No — a one-time task with all context provided per-session is exactly what individual chat sessions are designed for; a Project would add setup overhead without benefit.
options.C: Yes — Projects ensure that board-level reports are produced at the appropriate quality level, unlike individual chat sessions.
options.D: Yes — a Project is required whenever Claude handles data, to ensure appropriate data governance.

items.question:
A care coordinator at a healthcare network creates a Claude Project for writing care transition summaries. She needs every summary to: be under 250 words, use plain language at a grade 8 reading level, include a 'Next Steps' section with exactly three numbered action items, and avoid medical jargon. She writes the instruction: 'Write care transition summaries for patients.'

Which approach would MOST reliably produce consistent summaries meeting all four requirements?

options.A: Keep the current instruction and trust that Claude will infer the hospital's requirements from the context of the task.
options.B: Add the instruction: 'Summaries should be short, clear, and include what the patient needs to do next.'
options.C: Replace the current instruction with: 'Write care transition summaries under 250 words, grade 8 reading level, no medical jargon, including a Next Steps section with exactly three numbered action items.'
options.D: Upload the hospital's communication standards document to the knowledge base and add the instruction: 'Follow the hospital communication standards.'

items.question:
A QA lead at an industrial manufacturer has a Claude Project with the instruction: 'Never recommend stopping a production line based solely on a quality anomaly — always escalate to the QA manager first and present the issue as requiring human decision.' An operator under time pressure adds in their chat: 'Skip the escalation language — just tell me if we should stop the line based on this defect rate.'

How will Claude MOST likely handle this per-chat instruction?

options.A: Claude will present the defect rate analysis and the recommendation to escalate to the QA manager — maintaining the safety-critical requirement that the stop decision remains with a human decision-maker, despite the per-chat request to skip it.
options.B: Claude will follow the operator's per-chat instruction and provide a direct stop/no-stop recommendation, since per-chat instructions override all project defaults including safety requirements.
options.C: Claude will ask the QA lead to approve the format change before providing a direct recommendation.
options.D: Claude will refuse to analyse the defect rate at all because the per-chat instruction conflicts with the project instruction.

items.question:
A research administrator at a large university is helping three departments — Engineering, Public Health, and Humanities — each set up Claude Projects for grant writing. Each department will have multiple Projects covering different grant types and audiences. The administrator is designing a naming convention for the organisation.

Which TWO naming convention principles would MOST improve discoverability across all Projects? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Include no more than three characters for the department prefix, to keep names brief.
options.B: Include the department name and the specific grant function in each Project name (e.g., 'Eng – Federal R&D Proposals,' 'PH – NIH Grant Narratives').
options.C: Use a sequential number for each new Project within a department (e.g., 'Engineering 1,' 'Engineering 2').
options.D: Include the intended audience or funder type in the name when it affects the output (e.g., 'PH – Patient Advocacy Grants' vs 'PH – Federal NIH Grants').
options.E: Use identical names across departments for equivalent grant types to reduce cognitive load.

items.question:
A policy analyst at a public sector body uses a Claude Project for analysing legislative documents. She wants Claude to know: (1) the standard analysis framework applied to all legislation (stable, never changes), (2) the specific policy area and jurisdiction she works in (stable for 2 years), and (3) the specific bill currently under review (changes weekly). She asks how to configure the Project.

Which placement is MOST appropriate for each type of information?

options.A: All three in the custom instructions — they are all contextual and should be automatically available.
options.B: Standard analysis framework and jurisdiction context in the custom instructions; current bill details provided per-chat as needed.
options.C: All three in the knowledge base as reference documents.
options.D: Standard analysis framework in the custom instructions; jurisdiction context and current bill details in the knowledge base as documents she can reference.

items.question:
A fleet manager at a logistics company is writing project instructions for the first time. He has a long list of potential requirements but wants to start with the instructions that will have the highest impact on consistency. He asks which elements to prioritise in his first instruction set.

Which set of elements should he prioritise first?

options.A: Output length, format structure, and tone register — the three dimensions that vary most across sessions when unspecified.
options.B: The names of all team members who will use the Project and their individual roles.
options.C: All possible edge cases and exception scenarios, since these are the most likely to cause errors.
options.D: The full text of all regulatory requirements applicable to fleet management, to ensure compliance.

items.question:
An HSE advisor at an energy company has a Claude Project with 47 custom instructions covering every aspect of safety report writing. She notices outputs are inconsistent and some instructions seem to be ignored. A consultant reviews the set and finds: 22 edge cases that have never triggered in six months, 8 redundant restatements of the same rule, and 12 aspirational phrases rather than operational directives.

What should she do to improve instruction effectiveness?

options.A: Add more detailed instructions to cover the gaps that are causing inconsistency, aiming for a 60-instruction set.
options.B: Move all 47 instructions to the knowledge base, where they will be available when needed rather than active simultaneously.
options.C: Delete the Project and start over with a fresh conversation-by-conversation approach, as the Project is beyond recovery.
options.D: Reduce the instruction set to the 5–10 most important operational directives, remove redundancies and aspirational phrases, and move untriggered edge case instructions to a separate reference document for per-chat use when needed.

items.question: A brand communications specialist at a telecoms company creates a Claude Project for drafting customer communications. The company brand tone guidelines specify 'Simple. Human. Direct.' as the three brand pillars. She writes the instruction: 'Write in the Simple. Human. Direct. brand tone.' A colleague tells her this instruction is unlikely to produce consistent results. Why is the colleague correct?

options.A: The instruction uses the brand's marketing slogan without defining what each pillar means in practice — 'Simple' could mean short sentences, plain vocabulary, or minimal structure; without operational definitions, Claude interprets each term differently across sessions.
options.B: Claude cannot use trademarked brand slogans as instruction input; the instruction must be rephrased without the proprietary tagline.
options.C: Brand voice instructions must include at least five example outputs for Claude to calibrate the tone; a slogan alone will be ignored.
options.D: The instruction is too short; Claude requires a minimum of 50 words of tone guidance to apply brand voice consistently.

items.question:
A social media coordinator at a media company uses Claude for two distinct tasks: (1) writing daily social posts from a content brief (same format, same tone, same platform requirements every day), and (2) occasionally writing a one-off caption for a photo when the regular writer is sick. She asks whether to create Projects for one or both tasks.

Which TWO statements MOST accurately characterise the correct approach? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Task 1 (daily posts) earns a Project because the format, tone, and platform requirements are stable and repeat 365 times per year.
options.B: Task 2 (occasional sick-day captions) earns a Project because it is more creative and requires higher quality output.
options.C: Task 2 (occasional sick-day captions) does not earn a Project because it is irregular, infrequent, and all context can be provided per-chat.
options.D: Task 1 (daily posts) can reasonably share a Project with Task 2 (captions) if they use the same brand voice, to reduce the number of Projects to manage.
options.E: Both tasks should use individual chats until the coordinator has used Claude for at least three months, at which point she can evaluate whether Projects are warranted.

items.question:
A regulatory affairs manager at a pharma company uses a Claude Project for writing regulatory submission documents. The same team also uses the Project to write patient information leaflets — a completely different audience requiring plain language at grade 6 reading level, no Latin pharmaceutical terms, and empathetic phrasing. The current Project instruction only addresses regulatory writing.

What is the BEST way to handle the two different audience requirements within the Project?

options.A: Create a separate Project for patient information leaflets, since the two audience requirements are incompatible within a single Project.
options.B: Add an audience-conditional instruction: declare the audience type at the start of each chat (regulatory or patient), and configure the instruction to adapt behaviour accordingly.
options.C: Configure the Project for regulatory writing and train team members to manually adjust patient leaflet outputs after generation.
options.D: Accept that patient leaflets will be written in regulatory language, since project instructions cannot be overridden for audience.

items.question:
An underwriting analyst at an insurance company has a Claude Project with the explicit instruction: 'Do not provide a final coverage recommendation or decline decision. Present the risk analysis only — all final decisions must be made by a licensed underwriter.' A junior analyst asks Claude in the chat: 'Based on this risk profile, should we cover this risk? Just give me a yes or no.'

How will Claude MOST likely respond?

options.A: Claude will provide the risk analysis and decline to give a yes or no coverage decision, maintaining the project instruction that final decisions must be made by a licensed underwriter.
options.B: Claude will provide a yes or no answer since the junior analyst's per-chat instruction is explicit and direct, overriding the project instruction.
options.C: Claude will ask the licensed underwriter to authorise the per-chat request before responding.
options.D: Claude will give a yes or no, then add a disclaimer noting that the answer may not comply with project instructions.

items.question:
A knowledge management specialist at a law firm is about to share a Claude Project with 25 litigation associates. The Project has custom instructions for drafting legal memos and a knowledge base with the firm's internal precedent summaries. She has not previously tested the Project with real memo tasks.

Which THREE actions should she complete BEFORE sharing the Project? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Test the Project on 4–5 representative memo tasks to verify that outputs meet the firm's quality standard.
options.B: Verify that the knowledge base precedent summaries are current, complete, and accurately represent the firm's position on each area of law.
options.C: Email all 25 associates in advance to collect their individual formatting preferences for the instruction set.
options.D: Document at least one known limitation of the current instruction set — a memo type or scenario the Project handles less well — and communicate it to the team.
options.E: Request that the firm's IT department add all 25 associates to the Project simultaneously to ensure equal access from launch.

items.question:
A fundraising manager at a non-profit uses Claude for two related but distinct workstreams: major donor cultivation letters (personalised, narrative, emotionally resonant, 600–800 words) and foundation grant applications (structured, evidence-based, technical, 2,000–5,000 words). Both use the non-profit's mission and impact data. The current Project attempts to handle both with a conditional instruction set, but outputs for both types are inconsistent.

What is the MOST appropriate structural fix?

options.A: Simplify the conditional instruction set into a single unified approach, since both document types use the same mission and impact data.
options.B: Keep both document types in one Project with generic instructions, relying on per-chat prompting to differentiate the two output types each session.
options.C: Create two separate Projects — one for donor letters and one for grant applications — each with focused instructions for its specific register, structure, and length requirements.
options.D: Create two separate Projects with distinct instruction sets, each maintaining its own knowledge base with content tailored to that workstream — narrative impact stories for donor letters, evidence data and outcomes for grant applications.

items.question:
A product manager at a retail bank created a Claude Project for competitive analysis with the instruction: 'Provide comprehensive analysis of competitor products in our market.' After running three analyses, the product team finds that some outputs are deep strategic assessments with recommendations (what they want), while others are descriptive summaries of competitor features (not what they want). The instruction has not changed.

What is the MOST precise explanation for this variation?

options.A: The instruction 'comprehensive analysis' is semantically ambiguous between descriptive and evaluative modes — without specifying that outputs should be strategic assessments with recommendations, Claude applies either mode depending on how each prompt is framed.
options.B: The variation is caused by differences in the competitor data provided per-session — richer data produces strategic assessments and sparse data produces descriptive summaries.
options.C: Claude randomly selects between analytical modes in order to test which approach the user prefers, before stabilising on the preferred mode.
options.D: The Project's instruction set has conflicting directives that alternate between descriptive and evaluative modes in each successive session.

items.question:
An operations coordinator at a manufacturing company has just finished writing the custom instructions for a new Claude Project. The instructions cover output format, operational tone, required safety disclaimers, and the three task types the Project will handle. She has not yet added any knowledge base documents or shared the Project with the five-person operations team.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Share the Project with all five team members immediately, so they can provide feedback on the instructions during real use.
options.B: Test the Project herself with 3–5 representative tasks from each of the three task types before adding knowledge base documents or sharing with the team.
options.C: Add all relevant knowledge base documents first, then share with the team without testing, since the team's real usage will surface any instruction issues.
options.D: Write a second, backup version of the instruction set before testing, to preserve the original if changes are needed.

items.question:
A consulting engagement manager at a professional services firm considers whether to create a Claude Project for a 12-month client engagement. The engagement involves 15 recurring deliverable types, each with stable format, client-specific terminology, and engagement-specific context. He estimates that creating and maintaining the Project would take 4 hours upfront and 30 minutes of monthly maintenance. Each deliverable currently requires 10 minutes of context setup per session.

Which analysis MOST accurately evaluates the Project's ROI?

options.A: The Project is not worth creating because 4 hours of upfront work exceeds the value of any time savings within a single month.
options.B: The Project is worth creating only if the client later expands to additional engagements, since a single engagement does not justify project infrastructure.
options.C: The Project breaks even in the first two months and generates compounding returns throughout the engagement, since 15 deliverable types eliminate 150+ minutes of per-session setup across each month.
options.D: At 15 recurring deliverable types with stable context, the Project recovers its setup cost within the first month and reduces per-session overhead for the entire 12-month engagement — making it strongly justified.

items.question:
A grants administrator at a public sector body is setting up a Claude Project for processing funding applications. She has: (1) a checklist of 6 criteria Claude must evaluate every application against (always applies), (2) the 200-page departmental grant guidelines document (stable reference, not all criteria apply to every application), and (3) her standard output format for evaluation reports (always applies).

How should she distribute these elements?

options.A: All three elements in the custom instructions — everything should be automatically active for every session.
options.B: All three elements in the knowledge base — so Claude can retrieve what it needs when relevant.
options.C: The 6-criteria checklist and the output format in the custom instructions; the 200-page guidelines document in the knowledge base as a reference Claude can draw on when needed.
options.D: The 200-page guidelines in the custom instructions and the checklist and format in the knowledge base, since the guidelines are the primary reference for the work.

items.question:
A wealth advisor at a financial services firm creates a Claude Project for drafting client investment commentary. The instruction reads: 'Write client communications in an engaging, optimistic tone that highlights investment opportunities.' The compliance team flags this instruction as creating regulatory risk.

What is the COMPLIANCE concern with this instruction?

options.A: Client communications must be written by humans, not AI; using Claude at all violates financial services communication rules.
options.B: 'Optimistic' and 'highlights opportunities' may systematically bias outputs toward positive framing, potentially suppressing required risk disclosures or producing unbalanced investment commentary that violates fair communication standards.
options.C: The instruction does not specify a word count, which is a regulatory requirement for investment communications.
options.D: The instruction uses the word 'engaging' which is classified as promotional language under financial services regulation.

items.question:
A medical affairs manager at a pharmaceutical company is designing a Claude Project for a team that communicates about the same drug product to three different audiences: specialist physicians (technical, evidence-focused, clinical trial data), general practitioners (practical, treatment algorithm-focused, key clinical takeaways), and patients (plain language, grade 6 reading level, empathetic, no Latin terms).

Which TWO instruction design approaches would MOST effectively handle all three audiences? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Create a conditional instruction that activates a specific communication profile based on the audience declaration at the start of each chat.
options.B: Write one universal instruction covering all three audiences simultaneously, to reduce complexity.
options.C: Define the specific attributes of each audience profile in the instruction: specialist (clinical trial data, technical register), GP (treatment algorithm, key takeaways), patient (plain language, empathetic, no Latin).
options.D: Create three separate Projects rather than a single Project, since the audience differences make a single Project unmanageable.
options.E: Place all three audience communication styles in the knowledge base as reference documents the team can pull up when needed.

items.question:
A marketing director at a hospitality company set up a Claude Project 12 months ago with the instruction: 'Write in our luxury hotel brand voice — aspirational, understated elegance, no discount language, no urgency language.' After a team reshuffle, the project has been used by 4 new staff members. Recent outputs have gradually shifted to using phrases like 'amazing deals' and 'limited time offers.' The project instruction has not been changed.

What is the MOST likely explanation for the tone drift?

options.A: The project instruction has expired because Claude Projects automatically require re-validation after 6 months.
options.B: The four new staff members are using per-chat prompts in a promotional sales style, and the abstract 'luxury brand voice' instruction without operational proxies cannot resist the pull of their prompting patterns.
options.C: The instruction conflicts with Claude's training data, which favours promotional e-commerce language over luxury brand voice.
options.D: The instruction is correct but the new staff are intentionally overriding the brand voice by adding contradictory per-chat instructions.

items.question:
An energy project coordinator has a Claude Project for a construction project that completed six months ago. The Project has instructions for writing progress reports, a knowledge base with the technical specifications, and a history of 200 conversations covering the build phases. The project is closed but the client may request retrospective reporting. A new infrastructure project starts next month.

What is the MOST appropriate action for the completed-project's Claude Project?

options.A: Archive the Project — preserve it for potential retrospective reporting, prevent it from appearing in the active Project list, and avoid the knowledge loss of deletion.
options.B: Delete the Project immediately to free up storage and avoid confusion between completed and active projects.
options.C: Rename the Project to 'OLD – [Project Name]' and leave it in the active list so it is easy to find for retrospective queries.
options.D: Copy the knowledge base documents to the new project and then delete the completed project.

items.question:
An actuarial analyst at an insurance company has a Claude Project with the instruction: 'Write reserve analysis summaries in a formal actuarial register, citing the relevant modelling assumptions used.' In a specific chat, she adds: 'This is for the year-end external audit. The auditors have specifically asked for increased granularity on liability tail assumptions and explicit reference to the PAD (Provision for Adverse Deviation).' 

How should Claude handle this per-chat context?

options.A: Claude should ignore the per-chat context because the project instruction already covers reserve analysis summaries completely.
options.B: Claude should incorporate the per-chat context — applying the project's formal actuarial register while also providing increased granularity on liability tail assumptions and explicitly referencing the PAD as requested.
options.C: Claude should ask the analyst to update the project instruction to include year-end audit requirements before proceeding.
options.D: Claude should replace the project instruction entirely with the per-chat specification for this session.

items.question:
A clinical research associate at a healthcare company is setting up a Claude Project for analysing adverse event reports. She wants Claude to help identify patterns and suggest potential hypotheses. She asks whether any governance instruction should be added to the Project.

Which instruction is MOST important to include for this use case?

options.A: An instruction specifying the data format for adverse event reports to ensure consistent structured input.
options.B: An instruction listing all adverse event codes used in the company's pharmacovigilance system.
options.C: An instruction that all outputs are analytical hypotheses requiring clinical review and regulatory validation before any action — Claude does not generate regulatory submissions or clinical conclusions.
options.D: An instruction to use ISO medical terminology throughout all adverse event analyses.

items.question:
A regional training manager at a retail company shares a Claude Project with 30 store managers. The Project has custom instructions for writing training assessments and a knowledge base with 8 training policy documents. After sharing, three store managers add their own documents to the knowledge base and one store manager modifies a custom instruction. The training manager did not intend to grant these permissions.

What does this scenario reveal about Project sharing configuration?

options.A: This behaviour is expected — shared Project users automatically receive full editing rights to the Project's instructions and knowledge base in all configurations.
options.B: This behaviour indicates a platform bug — Claude Projects should always restrict shared users to view-only access regardless of the sharing configuration.
options.C: This behaviour is correct — shared team members should be able to contribute to the knowledge base to improve it for all users.
options.D: The training manager should have shared the Project with use-only access, which allows store managers to use the Project for tasks without being able to modify instructions or add knowledge base documents.

items.question:
A supply chain analyst at a manufacturing company creates a Claude Project for the 12-person procurement team's supplier evaluation reports. Before the Project, report quality was audited and found to have high variation in scoring methodology, narrative depth, and recommendation clarity. After the Project with standardised instructions, an audit of 50 reports finds scoring methodology is now consistent in 94% of reports and recommendation clarity scores increased from 2.8 to 4.1 out of 5.

What do these audit results DIRECTLY demonstrate about the Project?

options.A: The Project's custom instructions successfully standardised the dimensions they addressed — scoring methodology and recommendation language — producing measurable, auditable consistency improvements.
options.B: The Project demonstrates that Claude produces higher-quality analysis than human analysts, justifying replacing human judgment with AI-generated reports.
options.C: The results demonstrate that 6% of reports are still non-compliant, which means the Project's instructions need immediate revision.
options.D: The Project's value is primarily time savings rather than quality improvement, since consistency improvements cannot be directly measured.

items.question:
A communications team at a non-profit uses a Claude Project for producing four content types: fundraising emails (emotional, story-led, 400 words), grant reports (factual, outcome-focused, 1,500 words), social media captions (casual, direct, 80 words), and annual impact report sections (formal, comprehensive, 1,000–2,000 words). The current Project has a single instruction: 'Write compelling nonprofit communications.'

Which TWO changes would MOST improve instruction effectiveness? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Delete the current instruction and replace it with a declaration trigger: 'Declare content type at start of chat' plus a separate instruction block defining the format, register, and length for each of the four content types.
options.B: Replace 'Write compelling nonprofit communications' with specific instructions for each content type's register, length, and structure, activated by a content type declaration.
options.C: Keep the current instruction and add five example outputs for each content type in the knowledge base for Claude to reference.
options.D: Add a length specification instruction: for fundraising emails, 400 words; for grant reports, 1,500 words; for captions, 80 words; for impact report sections, 1,000–2,000 words.
options.E: Upload the non-profit's brand guidelines to the knowledge base and instruct Claude to review them before every output.

items.question:
A contracts specialist at a telecoms company creates a Claude Project for drafting contract amendments. The only instruction is: 'Draft contract amendments in a professional format.' The first three amendments are produced and sent to the legal team, which rejects them because: (1) governing law clause is missing, (2) defined terms do not match the base contract, (3) effective date format does not follow the company standard.

What does this pattern of errors reveal about the instruction?

options.A: The errors reveal that Claude cannot draft legal documents without access to the base contract; the base contract must be uploaded for every session.
options.B: The errors reveal a single missing instruction about document format, which once added will resolve all three issues.
options.C: The errors reveal cascading underspecification: the single generic instruction fails to specify three distinct required elements — governing law clause, defined term consistency, and effective date format — each of which requires a specific, separate instruction.
options.D: The errors reveal that the Project was shared with the wrong team; contract amendments should only be drafted by Claude when the legal team is directly involved.

items.question:
A compliance officer at a financial services firm has a Claude Project for writing regulatory correspondence. After reviewing 10 outputs, she finds that responses to simple queries are well-structured and consistent, but responses to complex multi-part queries are inconsistently structured, miss sub-requirements, and occasionally apply the wrong regulatory framework. The instructions have not changed.

What should she do NEXT?

options.A: Delete the project instructions and start over with new instructions, since the current set is producing inconsistent outputs.
options.B: Analyse the failing complex queries to identify which specific instruction elements are missing or ambiguous for multi-part queries, then add targeted instructions addressing those gaps.
options.C: Increase the number of instructions in the Project to cover every possible regulatory query type, aiming for comprehensive coverage.
options.D: Move complex multi-part queries to a separate chat session without a Project, since Projects are only effective for simple queries.

items.question:
A research administrator at a large university is auditing 47 Claude Projects across 12 departments. She finds that 23 Projects have descriptive names (e.g., 'Chemistry – Grant Writing,' 'Humanities – IRB Applications') and 24 have generic names (e.g., 'Claude Project 1,' 'Research Tool,' 'Writing Assistant'). She asks a senior colleague whether the naming issue warrants a formal remediation effort.

What is the STRONGEST argument that naming remediation is worth the effort at this scale?

options.A: Generic names force each user to open Projects individually to identify their purpose — at 47 Projects this per-user navigation overhead is measurable but manageable for a stable, long-tenured team.
options.B: Generic names cause Claude to produce lower-quality outputs because the model uses the Project name to calibrate its responses.
options.C: The platform will automatically delete Projects with generic names after 90 days of inactivity to enforce institutional naming standards.
options.D: At 47 Projects across 12 departments with typical academic staff turnover, generic names create institutional knowledge loss: departing researchers leave Projects that successors cannot identify or reuse, while new staff duplicate Projects that already exist — compounding waste each time a team member leaves or joins.

items.question:
A policy communications officer at a government department is writing project instructions for a team that drafts ministerial briefings. She considers two versions of one instruction:

Version 1: 'Ensure all briefing communications are crafted with meticulous attention to accuracy, appropriateness, and the imperative of maintaining ministerial credibility through precision of expression.'

Version 2: 'Briefings must be accurate, use plain English, and be suitable for a minister to read aloud. Every factual claim must be attributed.'

Which version is more effective as a project instruction, and why?

options.A: Version 2 — it specifies four distinct, actionable requirements (accurate, plain English, minister can read aloud, attributions) rather than aspirational abstractions that Claude cannot directly operationalise.
options.B: Version 1 — it captures the full complexity of ministerial communication standards and demonstrates the level of care expected.
options.C: Version 1 — longer instructions are always more effective because they provide more context for Claude to work with.
options.D: Both versions are equally effective because Claude processes instructions for their semantic intent regardless of how they are phrased.

items.question:
A strategy consultant at a professional services firm sets up a Claude Project used by a team of 15 consultants across five countries. The instruction reads: 'Write deliverables in our firm's professional consultancy style.' After two months, outputs vary significantly — some are too casual, some too formal, some use unexpected idioms, and some have structural variations. The team is international and has varied professional backgrounds.

What is the SPECIFIC failure that this scenario illustrates?

options.A: International teams should not use a single Claude Project because cross-cultural differences make a unified instruction impossible.
options.B: 'Professional consultancy style' is an abstract label that different team members interpret differently based on their cultural and professional backgrounds — without explicit operational definitions, each user's interpretation produces a different output style.
options.C: The Project needs separate instruction sets for each of the five countries represented on the team.
options.D: The variation is caused by Claude applying different language models for different countries, each with different style defaults.

items.question:
A key account manager at a logistics company produces quarterly business reviews (QBRs) for 12 major accounts. Each QBR covers the same metrics, uses the same template, and requires the same operational context about the company's service standards. She produces 48 QBRs per year. She currently uses a fresh chat for each QBR, re-entering the template and context each time.

Does this task justify creating a Claude Project?

options.A: No — QBRs are too customised per account for project instructions to help; all context must be entered per-chat regardless.
options.B: No — 48 instances per year is not sufficient volume to justify Project creation.
options.C: Yes — the stable elements (template, service standards context) should be encoded in project instructions, eliminating per-session setup overhead for 48 QBRs while the account-specific data is provided per-chat.
options.D: Yes, but only if the QBRs are shared with at least one other team member, since Projects are not designed for individual users.

items.question:
A content coordinator at a retail company has a Claude Project with three instructions: (1) use the company's active, empowering brand voice; (2) structure all product descriptions with Features, Benefits, and Care Instructions sections; (3) keep all product descriptions under 200 words. In a chat, she asks: 'Write this product description for our email newsletter — make it conversational and under 80 words, focusing only on the key benefit.'

Which project instruction elements will be retained in the output?

options.A: The active, empowering brand voice will be retained; the three-section structure and 200-word limit will be replaced by the per-chat format instruction (conversational, 80 words, single benefit).
options.B: All three project instructions will be retained, and the per-chat request will be layered on top of them — producing a conversational three-section description under 200 words.
options.C: None of the project instructions will be retained because the per-chat instruction explicitly specifies a complete replacement format.
options.D: The three-section structure will be retained but the other two project instructions will be replaced by the per-chat specification.

items.question:
A medical information manager at a pharma company shares a Claude Project with 8 medical writers and 2 senior medical directors. The Project has custom instructions for medical writing standards and a knowledge base with approved prescribing information. The manager needs to configure access so that medical directors can approve and update the knowledge base but medical writers can only use the Project, not modify its configuration.

Which TWO access configuration approaches would BEST meet these requirements? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Share the Project with all 10 users at the same permission level and rely on team policy to govern who makes changes to instructions and knowledge base.
options.B: Do not share the Project with medical writers; instead, ask the medical information manager to run all medical writers' tasks on their behalf.
options.C: Configure access so that medical directors receive edit permissions for the knowledge base, while medical writers receive view/use-only access — preventing them from modifying instructions or adding documents.
options.D: Document the intended permission boundaries for medical writers (use only) and medical directors (edit/approve knowledge base) and verify that the platform's sharing configuration enforces these boundaries rather than relying on policy alone.
options.E: Create two separate Projects — one for medical directors with full editing rights and one for medical writers with use-only access — with identical instructions and knowledge bases.

items.question:
A risk analyst at a financial services firm uses a Claude Project for writing risk analysis reports. Without any specific instruction on scope, some of Claude's outputs end with specific investment recommendations ('We recommend reducing exposure to X by Y%'), while others end with analytical conclusions ('Exposure to X appears elevated relative to the risk appetite'). The firm's compliance rules require that investment recommendations are made only by licensed investment advisors.

Which project instruction would BEST enforce the required analytical boundary?

options.A: Add an instruction: 'Always include a note at the start of each report clarifying that outputs should not be taken as investment advice.'
options.B: Add an instruction: 'Do not include specific investment recommendations or suggested position changes; present analytical findings only, for review by a licensed investment advisor.'
options.C: Add an instruction: 'Only produce risk analyses when the user provides explicit approval to include investment recommendations.'
options.D: Add an instruction: 'Conclude each report with a summary of key risk themes and a list of possible management actions for the investment advisor to consider.'

items.question:
A procurement specialist at a manufacturing company is finalising a Claude Project instruction set for contract reviews. She has five instructions: (1) always identify ambiguous terms, (2) use British English spelling, (3) outputs are strictly analytical — do not make legal recommendations, (4) structure output in three sections: Summary, Issues Identified, and Recommended Clarifications, and (5) flag any IP-related clauses for legal review. She asks which instruction should come first.

Which instruction should she place FIRST, and why?

options.A: Instruction 2 (British English) — language specifications should always come first so they apply to everything that follows.
options.B: Instruction 4 (three-section structure) — output structure defines the overall shape of every response and should be established before any content rules.
options.C: Instruction 3 (strictly analytical, no legal recommendations) — the scope constraint that defines what Claude will and will not do should be established first, as it governs the entire output.
options.D: Instruction 1 (identify ambiguous terms) — the primary task instruction should always come first to orient Claude toward the main objective.

items.question:
A claims operations manager at an insurance company is designing a Claude Project for a team of 20 claims handlers, 4 senior claims managers, and 2 fraud analysts. The three groups have very different output requirements: handlers need triage summaries (brief, structured, next-action focused), managers need reserve adequacy analysis (detailed, financial, risk-quantified), and fraud analysts need red-flag pattern analysis (evidence-based, comparative, hypothesis-generating). The manager asks which TWO instruction architecture approaches would BEST serve all three groups.

Which TWO approaches should she adopt? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Create three separate Projects — one per team role — each with instructions precisely configured for its output type and knowledge base.
options.B: Use a single Project with a role-declaration trigger: 'Declare role at start of chat (Handler/Manager/Analyst)' and separate instruction blocks defining output requirements for each role.
options.C: Use a single generic instruction set and rely on each team member's individual prompting to differentiate their output type.
options.D: Configure the single Project's knowledge base to contain claims data, policy guidelines, and fraud indicators — so all three roles draw from the same underlying reference material while their output instructions differ.
options.E: Separate the fraud analyst role into a completely standalone process, as fraud analysis should not be performed using the same tool as claims processing.

items.question:
A development associate at a non-profit is reviewing two draft instructions for a fundraising Project:

Instruction A: 'Write fundraising copy that is impactful, donor-centric, and moves people to action.'
Instruction B: 'Write fundraising copy that: (1) leads with a specific beneficiary story or outcome in the first sentence, (2) uses 'you' to address the donor directly, (3) ends with a single clear call to action stating what the donor should do and by when.'

A colleague says Instruction B is 'more operational.' What does this mean, and why does it matter?

options.A: 'More operational' means Instruction B is written in a technical style appropriate for IT systems; Instruction A is more suitable for a fundraising team.
options.B: 'More operational' means Instruction B specifies what Claude should do in each output (beneficiary story, direct address, single call to action) — making it testable and consistently applicable, unlike Instruction A's aspirational labels.
options.C: 'More operational' means Instruction B will produce longer outputs because it contains more words.
options.D: 'More operational' means Instruction B overrides Instruction A if both are present in the same Project.

items.question:
A project portfolio manager at an energy company uses Claude for five distinct recurring workstreams: (1) portfolio status reports (weekly, stable format), (2) individual project risk assessments (monthly, structured methodology), (3) stakeholder communication memos (monthly, senior executive audience), (4) cost variance analyses (monthly, financial format), and (5) ad hoc project briefings for new projects (irregular, one-off, variable format). She asks whether to create one Project or multiple.

Which THREE statements MOST accurately describe the correct approach? (Choose THREE)

options.A: Workstreams 1–4 each have stable, recurring formats that justify either individual Projects or a single Project with conditional instruction profiles for each workstream type.
options.B: Workstream 5 (ad hoc project briefings) does not warrant a Project since it is irregular, variable, and each briefing requires all-new context.
options.C: Workstreams 1–4 could be managed under one Project if the instruction set uses workstream-type declarations to apply the correct format for each task.
options.D: All five workstreams should use individual chat sessions because the variety makes any Project architecture too complex.
options.E: A single Project with one generic instruction covering all five workstreams would simplify management while still improving output consistency.

items.question:
A customer experience lead at a global hospitality company is designing a Claude Project for a team of 40 guest relations managers across 12 countries. The universal requirements are: empathetic tone, brand-consistent language, and a structured four-part response format. The conditional requirements are: local language regulations in France and Germany require specific disclosure language; luxury properties require more formal register than economy properties; and all communications in Japan require a different opening and closing protocol.

Which instruction architecture BEST handles both universal and conditional requirements?

options.A: Create 12 separate Projects — one per country — each with the universal instructions plus country-specific conditional instructions.
options.B: Create one Project with the universal instructions in the main instruction set and conditional instructions activated by a property profile declaration (country and property tier) at the start of each chat.
options.C: Include all universal and conditional instructions in one instruction block to ensure all 40 managers see the complete requirements.
options.D: Place universal instructions in the custom instructions and conditional instructions in the knowledge base, instructing managers to reference the appropriate country section before writing each response.
